modules.title: What an Ideology Is
modules.html:
An ideology is a coherent set of beliefs, ideas and ideals about how society should be organised, together with a programme for achieving that arrangement. Ideologies answer three questions: what is wrong with the present order, what an ideal order looks like, and how to get from one to the other.

Functions of ideology: it provides identity and cohesion for a group, guides policy choice, legitimises a regime, mobilises the masses for action, and offers a yardstick for criticising government.

Ideologies are commonly ranged from left (radical change, equality, collective ownership) through the centre (reform, mixed economy) to the right (order, hierarchy, private property).

examples.q: State two functions of ideology in a political system.
examples.a: (i) It provides a guide for making and justifying public policy. (ii) It mobilises citizens and gives a regime legitimacy by explaining and defending its programme.

modules.title: Communalism and Feudalism
modules.html:
Communalism is the earliest system of social organisation, found in pre-colonial African societies. Its features:

  • Land and major resources are owned collectively by the community or lineage, not by individuals.
  • Production is for use, not for profit; there is little or no surplus for exchange.
  • Labour is cooperative — age grades and work parties.
  • Absence of sharp class divisions; leadership by elders on behalf of all.
  • Strong extended-family and kinship obligations; a rudimentary welfare net.

Feudalism is a hierarchical, land-based system that dominated medieval Europe and appeared in northern Nigeria before colonial rule. Its features:

  • Ownership of land by a small class of lords; the serf or peasant works land he does not own.
  • Payment of tribute, rent or labour service in exchange for protection.
  • Rigid, hereditary social stratification: monarch → nobles → knights/vassals → serfs.
  • Political authority attached to landholding rather than to office.

examples.q: Identify one similarity and one difference between communalism and feudalism.
examples.a: Similarity: both are pre-industrial systems in which land is the central means of production. Difference: in communalism land is owned collectively with no exploiting class, while in feudalism land is monopolised by lords who extract tribute from serfs.

modules.title: Capitalism and Socialism Compared
modules.html:
BasisCapitalismSocialism
OwnershipPrivate ownership of the means of production.Public or collective ownership of the major means of production.
MotiveProfit maximisation.Social welfare and equality.
AllocationMarket forces of demand and supply; the price mechanism.Central planning by the state.
CompetitionFree competition among producers.State monopoly in key sectors.
Role of the stateMinimal (laissez-faire).Extensive and directive.
Class structureClass division between owners (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat).Aims at a classless society.
ExamplesUSA, Japan, Britain.Former USSR, Cuba, Tanzania under ujamaa.

Merits of capitalism: efficiency, innovation, consumer choice, individual freedom, reward for enterprise. Demerits: gross inequality, exploitation of labour, unemployment, boom-and-bust cycles, neglect of unprofitable social services.

Merits of socialism: reduction of inequality, security of employment, provision of welfare, planned use of resources. Demerits: bureaucratic inefficiency, absence of incentive, shortage of consumer goods, potential for political authoritarianism.

examples.q: Why is Nigeria described as operating a mixed economy?
examples.a: Because both private enterprise and public enterprise co-exist: individuals and companies own banks, factories and farms, while government owns or regulates strategic sectors such as petroleum, electricity transmission and the central bank.

modules.title: Communism, Fascism and Welfarism
modules.html:
Communism is the extreme form of socialism developed by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in The Communist Manifesto (1848). Key ideas: history is a series of class struggles; capitalism creates its own gravediggers in the proletariat; a revolution establishes a dictatorship of the proletariat; and eventually the state “withers away”, leaving a classless, stateless society governed by the principle “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.”

Fascism (Mussolini's Italy, 1922) and Nazism (Hitler's Germany, 1933) are extreme right-wing ideologies. Features: glorification of the state above the individual, one-party rule, an all-powerful leader, militarism and expansionism, suppression of opposition and free press, racialism (in the Nazi form), and corporatist control of the economy.

Welfarism holds that the state is responsible for the basic well-being of its citizens — free or subsidised education, health care, pensions, unemployment benefit — financed by progressive taxation while private enterprise continues. It is the middle way associated with Scandinavian countries and post-1945 Britain, and it underpins Chapter II of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution (Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy).

examples.q: According to Marx, what happens to the state under full communism?
examples.a: It withers away. Since the state is an instrument of class domination, once classes disappear the state loses its purpose and dissolves into an administration of things.

quiz.q: An ideology is best defined as
options: A set of beliefs about how society should be organised
quiz.solution: Ideology combines a diagnosis, an ideal and a programme.

quiz.q: Collective ownership of land in pre-colonial Africa illustrates
quiz.solution: Communalism features communal ownership and production for use.

quiz.q: In feudalism, the class that works land it does not own is the
quiz.solution: Serfs or peasants till the lord's land.

quiz.q: The chief motive of capitalism is

options: Public ownership of the major means of production
quiz.solution: Collective ownership is the core socialist principle.

quiz.q: 'From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs' describes
quiz.solution: It is the distributive principle of full communism.
Benito Mussolini founded fascism in Italy in 1922.

quiz.q: A distinguishing feature of fascism is
options: Glorification of the state and one-party rule
quiz.solution: The individual is wholly subordinated to the state.

quiz.q: An economy combining private and public ownership is
A major criticism of capitalism is
quiz.solution: Capitalism concentrates wealth and widens inequality.

quiz.q: A major criticism of socialism is
options: Lack of incentive and bureaucratic delay
quiz.solution: State planning can dull individual incentive.
Julius Nyerere's African socialism in Tanzania.

options: Provides for the basic well-being of citizens
quiz.solution: Welfare provision financed by taxation, alongside private enterprise.

quiz.q: Chapter II of the 1999 Constitution deals with
quiz.solution: It sets out welfare-oriented state objectives.

quiz.q: Marx argued that history is essentially a record of
quiz.solution: Historical materialism sees class struggle as the engine of history.
